Good m— good afternoon, Chair Banks, uh, and members of the Committee on Public Housing. My name is Metin Sarci. I serve as the Co-Chair of the Housing, Land Use, and Zoning Committee for Manhattan Community Board 9, and I am also an employee of the New York City Housing Authority. However, I am testifying today in my personal capacity, and the views expressed in this statement are my own and do not reflect official position or policy. In reviewing the Preliminary Budget, it appears that public housing residents are subjects in a perverse human experiment to determine how much weaponized incompetence is required to validate the destruction of their homes. We are witnessing a manufactured choice: place public assets under private enterprise, move them to a trust that works with a distrusted organization, or suffer the consequences. A vote for Section 9 should not be a vote for the status quo. It is a vote that says, I believe in public housing. The failure of the current Section 9 model is not a failure of the funding stream, but a

failure of stewardship. I am submitting a program proposal for a federally sanctioned solution that requires the, uh, built up of the Resident Management Corporations program. Unlike PACT or the trust, the RMC model professionalizes resident-led oversight within the Section 9 framework. By establishing this, uh, institutional capacity required under federal regulation, RMCs can mirror community boards while using public nonprofit solutions to address maintenance, security, and essential services. By utilizing HUD resident savings provisions, RMCs, unlike NYCHA, can retain operational surpluses for site-specific repairs, offering a vital cost avoidance strategy against the IBO projected budget gaps for FY ‘27 to ‘30. We must empower our residents who choose to stay in Section 9 with the professional tools to manage their own environments. I urge this Committee to support the RMC program as a legitimate third path solution for NYCHA's future, and I'll be sure to submit both, uh, presentations, program proposal, as well as any potential questions, uh, for the— for this Committee,

as well as any Council Members who are, uh, willing to listen about this particular program. Thank you.

It is the first team of legal advocates in New York City solely dedicated to representing public housing residents through the Right to Counsel program. We represent tenants in Section 9 and tenants in RAD/PACT developments in through right to counsel and through community clinics. For this reason, I think I have particular insight into the differences in the rights and protections that tenants experience in PACT and in Section 9. The city may need PACT for fiscal stability. That is clear from the earlier testimony that- that is their position. They need PACT for fiscal stability, but tenants living in these developments deserve stability as well. Year after

year, PACT landlords evict a larger percentage of residents than NYCHA. As any PACT tenant can tell you, and as many have already testified today, this is not because PACT developers are better managers. It is because of NYCHA's complete failure to create any actionable procedural rights or protections for PACT tenants, and then that leaves them without meaningful tools to solve problems or defend their tenancies, and it gives PACT landlords little to no incentive to resolve these cases rather than push for evictions. I've submitted written testimony that's much longer than my oral testimony today, and appended to that is a printout of the grievance and the lease termination procedures and rights included in NYCHA's ACOP for Section 9, and what's included in the Section 8 Administrative plan for PACT. You can see the stark disparity between the 2. One is about 2 pages. That's the Section 8 Admin plan, and the ACOP is multiple chapters. As an example, PACT tenants have the fewest succession rights out of any regulated housing in New York City, including Section 9, rent-stab, Mitchell-Lama, project-based Section 8, etc. Practically speaking,

this means that when the tenant of record dies, unless everything has gone perfectly up until that moment, remaining family members have no meaningful ability to fight for their home.
Uh, uh, 30 seconds— a minute to wrap up, sorry.

NYCHA can't evict somebody while that's pending. PACT landlords can. PACT is incredibly unpopular among tenants. As the city moves forward with these conversions, NYCHA must be required to create real parity between PACT and Section 9 tenant rights. Thank you for this opportunity.

Um, we are fighting for our lives and the future of public housing in New York City, and the fight begins with a clear demand: the city must commit the $662 million directly into Section 9 public housing, not PACT, not privatization schemes, but Section 9. It's the only structure that fully protects tenants' rights and keeps housing permanently public. What we are witnessing today is not accidental. Landlords and developers have learned from one another, and residents are paying the price. Repairs take longer, vendors fail to deliver, and living conditions decline, all while accountability disappears. NYCHA, which should be overseeing these processes, has failed to provide meaningful oversight. We have already seen this pattern play out in cases where companies cycle through

developments without consequence, better known as, what, Penrose kicking out Pinnacle and then Pinnacle somehow ending up in West Brighton. So we continue to— they continue to profit while residents deal with the fallout. This is not accountability, it is a revolving door. At the same time, the city continues to claim it supports social housing while actively shifting it into private hands. That contradiction is not also in the residents who have built and sustained communities like Chelsea. We are the people who stayed through disinvestment, through neglect, through decades when public housing was ignored. Now at Fulton and Elliott Chelsea, we are being asked to accept the plan that will consolidate us into 3 buildings per campus while handing over the majority of our land to so-called affordable housing that is not affordable to us, or frankly, most people in New York City. Along with luxury housing. When low-income housing is defined as serving households earning $56,000 to $90,000 a year, we must ask, affordable to whom? And what will, and what will the range look like in 10 or 20 years? These policies are not designed for the residents who live

here now. We must also confront how these plans are being financed. Project-based Section 8 is being used to fund the demotion of public housing. Yet Section 8 itself is not a stable system. Federal funding for the program has repeatedly threatened, and the expiration of the Emergency Housing Voucher program has already shown how fragile these supports are. NYCHA has issued vouchers without long-term guarantees to sustain them, placing residents into an increasingly uncertain system. Moving people out of permanent public housing under Section 9 and into a precariously privately controlled rent control system is not a solution. It is transfer of risk onto tenants. Alongside the structural shift, residents are experiencing direct pressure. Companies like Related Affordable Management have engaged— has engaged in aggressive tactics, knocking on doors, sending repeated texts and emails targeting tenants in Phase 1. Residents have already seen what happened at Fulton and Chelsea Addition, and the same patterns are emerging again. This is not engagement, it is harassment. It is compounded by broader pressures

from Housing Opportunities Unlimited, NYCHA planners and officials who continue to push this process forward despite clear resident opposition. The reality is that the driving force behind this decision is not the condition of the buildings, but the value of the land. That was stated when Alexa Avilés, when she was Chair, simply asked Simon Klawitzke for the metrics, and he said, it's actually the land value of Chelsea. Needless to say, this will continue. At the same time, the city claims NYCHA is underfunded, yet thousands of units sit unused. More than 6,000 apartments remain vacant alongside 3,000 non-dwelling units. This represents loss of rent and lost subsidy, resources that could and should be invested into public housing. Instead of addressing this inefficiency, the focus remains on privatization. Funding alone is not enough. There must be strict accountability for how funds are spent. Public money must not be diverted into structures like the trust that move housing further away from public control. Instead, funding must be directed

toward real capital improvement, repairs, infrastructure, and rehabilitation of existing units. In our case, residents are being—
30 seconds to wrap it up.

So we ask simple— something very simple. NYCHA residents are often spoken about as symbols used to represent resilience or diversity, which our actual voices are ignored. When public housing is harmed, it is not an abstract policy failure. It is direct harm to people whose labor sustains this city. We are the workers, caregiving families who make New York function, even as we remain invisible in its politics.

Good afternoon. This is a statement to the New York City Council Public Housing

Committee regarding the federal cuts to NYCHA and the need for dedicated city budget item line. Good afternoon, Chairman Banks and members of the Committee. On behalf of the Citywide Council of Presidents, my name is Reginald Bowman, and I serve as the business manager for the Citywide Council of Presidents, representing most and more than— more than 500,000 NYCHA residents across 335 developments citywide. Chairman Banks, we appreciate your continued leadership and advocacy for public housing residents, and we come before you today with urgency and a clear call to action. The recently proposed 14% cut in federal funding to NYCHA comes at a time when the authority is already facing a capital need exceeding $78 billion, according to NYCHA's 2023 fiscal needs assessment. This is not theoretical, this is structural disinvestment. Indeed, federal law under the U.S. Housing Act of 1937 established public housing as a federal responsibility, and regulations such as 24 CFR Part 990 govern operating subsidies meant to sustain developments. Yet federal appropriations

have consistently fallen short of these obligations, leaving NYCHA underfunded by billions over decades. As a result, NYCHA receives less than 90% of its federally authorized operating subsidy in most years. We all know critical systems, heat, elevators and plumbing continue to deteriorate, and as you've heard today, residents continue to endure conditions that in many cases fall below the standards outlined in HUD's Housing Quality Standards 24 CFR 703. Somebody called it today a white-collar ripoff. Therefore, Chairman Banks, This is where the city must step in, not as a temporary fix, but as a permanent partner. We, the Citywide Council of Presidents, are calling on the New York City Council to establish a dedicated baseline item in the city budget for NYCHA for both operating and capital support. This request is grounded not only in need but in precedent and policy authority. Under the New York City— wrap it up in 30 seconds— under the New York City Section 254, the Council has the power to adopt and modify the city's budget to address essential public needs. Housing, particularly for over half a

million low-income residents, meets the and exceeds that threshold. Additionally, the city already supplements NYCHA through programs such as the NYCHA operating subsidy support, the Mayor's Action Plan for Housing, but these are discretionary and inconsistent. What we want now is codified guaranteed funding. A dedicated line item would stabilize NYCHA against unpredictable federal cuts, ensure compliance with federal habit— habitability standards, strengthen workforce capacity and response times, and provide transparency and accountability in funding, which we haven't been getting much from NYCHA. Without this, we remain in a reactive posture managing crisis instead of delivering sustainability. So Chairman Banks, the residents of NYCHA— we, the residents of NYCHA, are not invisible and we're not optional. We are seniors, families, veterans, and essential workers and economic anchor who uphold this city and continue to uphold this city through its most difficult times, from COVID-19 to today's affordability crisis to what we hear happening now all over the city.

The question before us is simple, as I wrap up: will New York City match its values with investment? We therefore urge this Committee, under your leadership, to take bold legislative and budgetary action to create a permanent NYCHA line item. Let this be the moment where the city affirms that public housing is not just a federal responsibility but a New York City priority. Thank you, Chairman Banks, and we look forward to working with you to get this done.
